prompt:
You run weekly onboarding A/B tests. Here is every finished test so far: what you predicted
and what was measured.

- round 1: Photo Quality Assistant and Real-Time Pet Preview [adoption, redesign]: predicted +14.0%, measured -17.0% ± 4.3%, after noise correction -7.2%, stopped early: adoption worse
- round 2: Late Sign-In After Pet Adoption [sign_in, reorder]: predicted +6.0%, measured -16.6% ± 4.3%, after noise correction -7.2%, stopped early: sign_in worse

By kind of change, after noise correction:
- adoption, redesign: -7.2% after noise correction, 1 test(s) (one test only: weak evidence, not a pattern yet)
- sign_in, reorder: -7.2% after noise correction, 1 test(s) (one test only: weak evidence, not a pattern yet)

One test is weak evidence. State a rule only when at least 2 tests of that kind agree after noise correction; otherwise say the evidence is still thin.

Previous lessons:
Evidence is still thin to establish rules on which changes work or prediction accuracy.

Rewrite the lessons: at most 6 short rules about which kinds of change worked, which did not, and
where your predictions were too high or too low. Call a kind of change helpful only if a test of that
kind won (was significant); for tests with no clear effect, say no effect was seen, even if the numbers
lean one way. Keep rules that still hold, drop ones the data contradicts. Return JSON {"lessons": ["..."]}

lessons: Evidence is still thin to establish rules on which kinds of change work or fail, as each kind of change has only one test.
Predictions were consistently too high: both tests predicted positive gains (+14.0% and +6.0%), but both resulted in negative outcomes (-7.2% after noise correction).
